query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy, the addition of 5 at% aluminum combined with an aging heat treatment at 800 °C for 1 hour will induce the formation of finely dispersed coherent Ni3Ti-type (γ′) nanoprecipitates, resulting in an approximate 20% increase in elevated-temperature yield strength compared to an identical alloy lacking this intervention.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, as-cast Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy with principal elements present in the 5–35 at% range (e.g., ~35 at% Ti, ~35 at% Ni, and the balance distributed among other elements), exhibiting a single-phase microstructure with limited precipitation hardening.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of 5 at% aluminum into the baseline composition, followed by an aging heat treatment at 800 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere to activate precipitation of the γ′ phase.
generation.conditions: The intervention is to be performed at 800 °C for 1 hour under an inert or vacuum atmosphere to prevent oxidation; the alloy composition must continuously respect the 5–35 at% rule for principal elements.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense and uniformly distributed population of coherent Ni3Ti-type (γ′) nanoprecipitates within the primary matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening through the formation of coherent, ordered nanoprecipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation motion, particularly at elevated temperatures, thereby increasing the yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the same Ti-Ni primary HEA without the intervention, the treated alloy will exhibit an elevated-temperature yield strength increase on the order of approximately 20%, while maintaining adequate ductility.
generation.baseline: The same Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy produced without the 5 at% Al addition and subsequent aging heat treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for alloys within the compositional bounds of 5–35 at% per element and for elevated-temperature operation around 800 °C. Deviation from the specified Al content or aging conditions may not yield the desired precipitate volume fraction and strengthening effect.
generation.uncertainty: Variability in precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction may affect the magnitude of strength improvement. Process variations in heat treatment and slight compositional fluctuations could lead to experimental deviations from the predicted ~20% improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti- and Ni-primary HEA samples: one set with the baseline composition and one set with 5 at% Al addition. Subject the Al-containing samples to an aging heat treatment at 800 °C for 1 hour. Characterize the microstructure using TEM or SEM to verify the presence of coherent Ni3Ti-type (γ′) nanoprecipitates. Then perform tensile tests at elevated temperatures (approximately 800 °C) to compare yield strengths between the two sets.
measurements: High-resolution microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) for precipitate identification and size distribution.
Elevated-temperature tensile tests to quantify yield strength and ductility.
XRD analysis to confirm phase composition.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added, aged alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant (approximately 20% or greater) increase in yield strength at 800 °C relative to the baseline alloy, or if TEM/SEM fails to detect a coherent population of Ni3Ti-type (γ′) nanoprecipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of elements with similar metallic atomic radii but different crystallographic structures (Al and Ti) to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy caused higher solution strengthening by the element with a different crystallographic structure than the solvent. The solid solution strengthening coming from addition of 5 at. pct Al to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy is negligible, while the addition of 5 at. pct of Ti significantly increases the solid solution strengthening. The precipitation hardening effect related to the presence of (CoNi)3Ti phase caused by the addition of 5 at. pct Ti is comparable with the total effect of the 5 at. pct Al and 5 at. pct Ti addition, which caused the precipitation of γ′ ((NiCo)3AlTi). Precipitation hardening is much greater in the investigated alloys than the solid solution hardening. We showed a successful way for effectively strengthening the FCC-HEA system (NiCoFe) using a small Ti addition. The microstructure obtained in the M3 alloy consists of precipitates with an L12 structure and structurally coherent with FCC matrix. We showed one of the ways of searching for new high-entropy alloys.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. First, our selected strengthening phases are ductile, highly coherent and low misfit with matrix (i.e. they can compatibly deform with the matrix), implying that increasing their content does not significantly degenerate the ductility. Controllable microstructure (by either alloying or processing design) provides numerous possibilities for the optimization of properties; for instance, the strength of our alloy can be controlled within a very wide range, at least, of ~270–1900 MPa, and the largest elongation is >40%. Furthermore, benefiting from the advantages of the multi-principal-element/high-entropy matrix, high Cr addition can improve the resistance to corrosion and oxidation, and high Al content reduces the alloy density. These advantages present the potential for the application of our HEA to many rigorous service conditions, such as those subjected to very large loading and involving highly corrosive environment. The identified mechanical properties of the as-cast MEAs are presented in Table 3 and Figure 3, which reveal that all the as-cast MEAs exhibited similar levels of hardness (approximately Hv 320–330). However, the yield strength and ductility of these as-cast MEAs exhibited an increasing trend when their Zr content was increased. The small increases in yield strength (approximately 3–8%) were consistent with the hardness variation results. The Zr additions were presumed to increase the grain sizes of MEA ingots, which reduced their yield strength and, therefore, compensated for the effect of solid solution strengthening achieved through Zr additions. Accordingly, to further improve the mechanical properties of the MEAs, their microstructure (e.g., fine grain or heterostructure) must be modified through thermomechanical treatment (TMT). Therefore, the as-cast Zr7 MEA, which had an optimum combination of yield strength and ductility, was selected for further processing through TMT.

papers.title: Manufacturing of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti High-Entropy Alloy Using Directed Energy Deposition and Evaluation of Its Microstructure, Tensile Strength, and Mic
papers.system: Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA (with design emphasis on γ + γ′ phases)
papers.approach: Directed energy deposition (DED) was used to fabricate an alloy with controlled Al and Ti content, aiming to form a primary FCC γ matrix with finely dispersed, ordered γ′ precipitates.
papers.findings: A well‐designed Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti alloy formed a Ni-rich FCC matrix (γ phase) with a uniformly distributed, ordered γ′ phase. This dual‐phase microstructure provided enhanced tensile strength, hardness, and thermal stability, particularly around elevated temperatures (~800 °C).
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via formation of coherent, ordered Ni3(Ti,Al)-type precipitates within an FCC matrix increases elevated-temperature yield strength by impeding dislocation motion.

papers.title: The Effect of Al and Ti Additions on Solid Solution Strengthening and Precipitation Hardening in CoNiFe Medium-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Co-Ni-Fe medium-entropy alloy enhanced by Al and Ti additions
papers.approach: Minor additions of Ti (and Al) were incorporated into the CoNiFe system to promote the formation of ordered strengthening phases (such as (CoNi)3Ti or γ′) alongside benefiting from solid solution effects.
papers.findings: While 5 at.% Al had a negligible effect on solution strengthening, adding 5 at.% Ti significantly increased the alloy’s yield strength through precipitation hardening. The formation of an L12-ordered (NiCo)3AlTi phase resulted in substantial strength gains.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation hardening dominates over solid solution strengthening in these systems; the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates (in an L12 structure) acts as obstacles to dislocation glide.

papers.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Non-equiatomic HEA tailored with high Ni (and by implication Ti) content
papers.approach: A composition with a high Ni/Al ratio was designed so that spinodal decomposition in situ produces a near-equiatomic FCC matrix with high-content, ductile, coherent Ni3Al-type (γ′) nanoprecipitates.
papers.findings: The developed alloy displayed an impressive strength increase (~1.5 GPa improvement, reaching 1.9 GPa tensile strength) with retained good ductility. Although the study emphasized room‐temperature behaviors, the same mechanisms are expected to contribute to high-temperature strength.
papers.mechanism: Spinodal order–disorder decomposition leads to the formation of low-misfit, coherent nanoprecipitates that interact with dislocations (via diffuse obstacles and creation of antiphase boundaries), thereby greatly enhancing strength.

papers.title: Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions.
papers.system: TiAlCrNbV medium-entropy alloy with minor Zr additions
papers.approach: By adding small amounts of Zr into a Ti-rich MEA and applying thermomechanical processing routes (such as hot rolling followed by cold rolling and rapid annealing), the study aimed to modulate both the grain size and solid solution effects.
papers.findings: While Zr increased the grain size in as-cast samples (partially offsetting solid solution strengthening), appropriate thermomechanical treatments significantly refined the microstructure. This resulted in an optimal balance with increased ductility and reasonably maintained yield strength.
papers.mechanism: A balance between solid solution strengthening by Zr (through lattice distortion) and grain refinement (via dynamic recrystallization) influences the alloy’s high-temperature performance.

papers.title: The Microstructures, Mechanical Properties, and Deformation Mechanism of B2-Hardened NbTiAlZr-Based Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: NbTiAlZr-based refractory HEAs (with primary constituents including Ti and Ni is analogously relevant)
papers.approach: Casting alloys with designed B2 ordered matrices and controlled addition of Zr to leverage solid solution effects were studied.
papers.findings: The alloys exhibited excellent room-temperature plasticity and favorable specific yield strengths at elevated temperatures (e.g., SYS ~131 MPa·cm3/g at 1023 K). The strengthening was ascribed mainly to the solid solution effect (particularly from larger atoms like Zr) and to dislocation slip characteristics in the B2 matrix.
papers.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening from atomic size misfit, combined with characteristic dislocation slip (planar slip along specific orientations), provided enhanced high-temperature mechanical properties.

established: Precipitation strengthening via formation of coherent, ordered nanoprecipitates (e.g., γ′ or Ni3(Ti,Al) phases) significantly enhances yield strength at elevated temperatures.
In many HEA systems, fine-tuning the alloy composition (especially the Al+Ti balance) is crucial for controlling phase formation and thermal stability.
Solid solution strengthening and lattice distortion (from elements like Zr) can further contribute to strength, although grain structure and processing routes play important roles.
Spinodal decomposition strategies have been shown to generate high-content, ductile nanoprecipitates without sacrificing ductility.

approaches_tried.approach: Adding Al (and tuning the Al/Ti ratio) to promote a dual-phase γ + γ′ microstructure in Ni-rich HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Formation of finely dispersed, ordered precipitates that substantially improve yield strength and high-temperature properties

approaches_tried.approach: Introducing minor Zr in Ti-rich medium-entropy alloys, coupled with thermomechanical processing
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved grain refinement through hot rolling and increased ductility; modest yield strength improvement that depends on balancing solid solution effects versus grain coarsening

mechanisms: Precipitation hardening through the formation of coherent, ordered (γ′) nanoprecipitates that obstruct dislocation glide
Spinodal decomposition resulting in a nanophase-separated structure with diffuse obstacles and antiphase boundaries
Solid solution strengthening from atomic size misfit and lattice distortion effects
Grain boundary strengthening via thermomechanical treatment and dynamic recrystallization
disagreements: There is some debate over the relative contributions of solid solution versus precipitation strengthening in different HEA systems; while some studies emphasize the dominant role of precipitation (especially in dual-phase alloys), others point to the key role of grain refinement and lattice distortion.

The optimal balance between ductility and strength (especially at elevated temperatures) remains unsettled, with varying processing routes (e.g., cold rolling vs. hot rolling) yielding different trade-offs.
open_questions: What are the detailed effects when both Ti and Ni become primary constituents (as opposed to one acting as an addition) on phase stability and high-temperature properties?
Can the precipitation processes be precisely controlled (through minor alloying additions and processing) to maximize elevated-temperature yield strength while maintaining ductility?
How can the interplay between solid solution strengthening, precipitation hardening, and grain size effects be optimized in a Ti- and Ni-primary HEA to fully exploit its high-temperature potential?
opportunities: Investigate a controlled intervention in a Ti-Ni-primary HEA by adding a small, well‐defined amount of a minor alloying element (e.g., Al) to deliberately induce fine, coherent precipitation of a γ′ phase (such as Ni3Ti) at elevated temperature.
Employ rapid solidification and tailored thermomechanical processing (e.g., DED followed by specific annealing cycles) to achieve finer grain and precipitate distributions.

Combine insights from precipitation and spinodal decomposition strategies to optimize the balance between strength and ductility in Ti- and Ni-rich HEAs, particularly targeting operating conditions above 800 °C.

Design an experiment where the intervention (small Al addition to promote fine ordered precipitates) is compared directly with the base Ti-Ni alloy, with explicit metrics (e.g., yield strength, ductility) measured at elevated temperatures that, if not met, would falsify the hypothesis.

directions.direction: Composition design by minor alloying addition of aluminum to promote in situ formation of coherent Ni3Ti‐type (γ′) nanoprecipitates.
directions.assessment: This approach directly attacks the limitation by enabling precipitation strengthening in a Ti- and Ni-primary HEA. It builds on well‐established physics of γ′ formation (as in Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti systems) and evidence from studies that show that small Al additions drive ordering and coherent precipitation [PMC11396108, PMC10532893]. The physics of coherent precipitate strengthening is well understood and practically feasible using controlled aging heat treatments.

directions.direction: Tailored thermomechanical processing (e.g. controlled hot rolling and precise aging treatment) to refine grain size and optimize precipitate distribution.
directions.assessment: This strategy would control both the grain structure and the dissolution–reprecipitation kinetics. While it indirectly supports precipitation strengthening by refining the microstructure, it may require complex processing conditions and may interact with composition in non‐linear ways.

directions.direction: Incorporation of minor solute elements such as zirconium to enhance solid solution strengthening and possibly induce beneficial grain boundary segregation.
directions.assessment: Zr additions have been shown to refine grains and provide lattice distortion effects [PMC9506522]. However, Zr may increase grain size when added in high amounts and its effects might be less targeted than directed precipitation strengthening in promoting elevated-temperature yield strength.

directions.direction: Surface modification (e.g., application of oxidation‐resistant coatings) to protect against high‐temperature degradation and thereby indirectly improve mechanical performance.
directions.assessment: While such coatings can improve oxidation resistance and hence durability at elevated temperatures, they do not directly address the intrinsic yield strength or plasticity improvements desired in the bulk alloy.

directions.direction: Atomistic modeling and simulation to predict optimal phase separation and precipitation kinetics in a Ti–Ni primary HEA, guiding subsequent experimental validation.
directions.assessment: Computational design could provide insights but would only be indirectly useful without experimental validation. It is informative but does not by itself constitute a single testable intervention in the material’s processing.

choice.direction: Composition design by minor alloying addition of aluminum to promote in situ formation of coherent Ni3Ti‐type (γ′) nanoprecipitates.
choice.why: Because the evidence shows that controlled small additions of Al in Ni- and Ti-containing HEA systems can trigger the formation of coherent, ordered nanoprecipitates (γ′ phase) that significantly strengthen the alloy at elevated temperatures. This approach directly targets the mechanism of precipitation strengthening, is supported by established research [PMC11396108::web::000::abstract, PMC10532893::web::019::5_conclusions, PMC6170471::web::013::discussion], and is relatively straightforward to implement experimentally.
